cards.front: How does a Wnt signal raise the level of free cytoplasmic β-catenin in a cell?
cards.back: Cells make β-catenin continuously and destroy free copies soon after; Wnt raises free β-catenin by slowing that constant destruction rather than increasing synthesis.
cards.why: This mechanism applies to free cytoplasmic β-catenin, not the stable cadherin-bound junctional pool.
cards.quote: Wnt raises free β-catenin by slowing its constant destruction; planar polarity aligns cells as neighbours sort Frizzled to one edge.

cards.front: Outside Wnt signaling, β-catenin has a stable structural role linking {{c1::cadherins}} to the cytoskeleton at cell junctions.
cards.quote: β-Catenin has a second, stable job linking cadherins to the cytoskeleton at cell junctions.
cards.section: Marking free β-catenin for destruction

cards.front: What are the four proteins of the β-catenin destruction complex, and what does each do?
cards.back: Axin is the scaffold, APC binds β-catenin for efficient ubiquitination handover, and CK1 and GSK3 are the two kinases.
cards.quote: the scaffold Axin (as in adaptors-and-scaffolds), the large protein APC (which binds β-catenin and is required for efficient ubiquitination handover) and two kinases, CK1 and GSK3.
cards.section: Marking free β-catenin for destruction

cards.front: In the β-catenin destruction complex, why must CK1 phosphorylate β-catenin before GSK3 acts?
cards.back: GSK3 prefers a substrate already phosphorylated four residues toward the C-terminus, so CK1 must add a priming phosphate first.
cards.why: CK1 phosphorylates serine 45, enabling GSK3 to step back in fours across threonine 41, serine 37, and serine 33.
cards.quote: Their order matters because GSK3 prefers a target already phosphorylated four residues toward the C-terminus.
cards.section: Marking free β-catenin for destruction

cards.front: In the destruction complex, CK1 phosphorylates {{c1::serine 45}} of β-catenin, priming GSK3 to step back in fours across threonine 41, serine 37, and serine 33.
cards.quote: CK1 phosphorylates serine 45, priming GSK3 to step back in fours across threonine 41, serine 37 and serine 33.
cards.section: Marking free β-catenin for destruction

cards.front: Which subunit of the SCF E3 ubiquitin ligase selects phosphorylated β-catenin for ubiquitination, and which phosphorylated sites does it read?
cards.back: β-TrCP, the substrate-recognition subunit of SCF, reads phosphoserines 33 and 37 on β-catenin.
cards.quote: β-TrCP, the substrate-recognition subunit of an SCF E3 ubiquitin ligase (ubiquitin-and-proteolysis), reads phosphoserines 33 and 37, SCF adds ubiquitin, and the proteasome degrades β-catenin.
cards.section: Marking free β-catenin for destruction

cards.front: In a cell receiving no Wnt, what sequence of steps clears free cytoplasmic β-catenin?
cards.back: The destruction complex phosphorylates free β-catenin, an SCF E3 ubiquitin ligase tags it with ubiquitin, and the proteasome degrades it.
cards.quote: Then SCF targets β-catenin: β-TrCP, the substrate-recognition subunit of an SCF E3 ubiquitin ligase (ubiquitin-and-proteolysis), reads phosphoserines 33 and 37, SCF adds ubiquitin, and the proteasome degrades β-catenin.
cards.section: Marking free β-catenin for destruction

cards.front: A mutation alters serine 45 of β-catenin so it cannot be phosphorylated, while threonine 41, serine 37, and serine 33 remain intact. Without Wnt, what happens to free β-catenin, and why?
cards.back: Free β-catenin accumulates without Wnt. Without CK1's priming phosphate at serine 45, GSK3 is not primed to step back across residues 41, 37, and 33, so serines 33 and 37 stay unphosphorylated and β-TrCP cannot bind to trigger SCF ubiquitination.
cards.quote: Without CK1's priming phosphate at serine 45, GSK3 is not primed to step back through 41, 37 and 33.
cards.section: Marking free β-catenin for destruction

cards.front: Under constant synthesis and unsaturated, first-order destruction, steady level of β-catenin = rate of synthesis ÷ {{c1::rate constant of destruction}}.
cards.quote: Under the first-order scope above: steady level of β-catenin = rate of synthesis ÷ rate constant of destruction
cards.section: Marking free β-catenin for destruction

cards.front: Why does regulating β-catenin via constant synthesis and variable destruction let the cell switch levels rapidly in both directions?
cards.back: Because synthesis is already running, free β-catenin starts rising as soon as destruction slows, and clears quickly once destruction resumes.
cards.quote: Because synthesis is already running, free β-catenin starts to rise as soon as destruction slows, and clears quickly when destruction resumes.
cards.section: Marking free β-catenin for destruction

cards.front: In the first-order turnover model of free β-catenin, synthesis stays constant at 20 molecules per minute while Wnt slows the destruction rate constant from 0.5 per minute to 0.05 per minute. What are the steady levels before and after Wnt, and by what factor does β-catenin rise?
cards.back: Steady level = rate of synthesis ÷ rate constant of destruction. Without Wnt: 20 ÷ 0.5 = 40 molecules. With Wnt: 20 ÷ 0.05 = 400 molecules. Slowing destruction 10-fold raises the steady level 10-fold without changing synthesis.
cards.quote: Slow destruction ten-fold (say from 0.5 to 0.05 per minute at constant synthesis) and the steady level rises ten-fold without changing synthesis.
cards.section: Marking free β-catenin for destruction

cards.front: A researcher blocks protein synthesis in cultured cells and finds that half of free β-catenin disappears in 10 minutes without Wnt and in 60 minutes with Wnt, while synthesis rate is unchanged. Under first-order destruction, by what factor does Wnt raise the steady level of β-catenin?
cards.back: It raises the steady level 6-fold. For first-order decay, the rate constant equals ln 2 ÷ half-life, so lengthening half-life 6-fold (10 to 60 minutes) lowers the destruction rate constant 6-fold; with synthesis constant, steady level (= synthesis ÷ rate constant) rises 6-fold.
cards.quote: steady level of β-catenin = rate of synthesis ÷ rate constant of destruction
cards.section: Marking free β-catenin for destruction

cards.front: In the Wnt-producing cell, the enzyme {{c1::Porcupine}} attaches a fatty acid to a serine residue on Wnt.
cards.quote: Wnt is an unusual secreted protein carrying a fatty acid that Porcupine attaches to a serine in the producing cell.
cards.section: How Wnt slows destruction and flips TCF

cards.front: Why does secreted Wnt act mostly as a short-range signal in many tissues?
cards.back: Its attached fatty acid makes Wnt cling to membranes and hard to dissolve, limiting how far it spreads from the producing cell.
cards.why: In the crystal structure of Wnt bound to Frizzled's outer domain, the fatty acid also sits in a receptor groove as part of the binding grip.
cards.quote: That lipid makes Wnt cling to membranes, hard to dissolve, and mostly short-range in many tissues.
cards.section: How Wnt slows destruction and flips TCF

cards.front: Which two membrane proteins form the receptor complex that Wnt brings together on a target cell, and what are their membrane topologies?
cards.back: Frizzled, a seven-pass membrane protein, and its co-receptor LRP5 or LRP6, a single-pass membrane protein.
cards.quote: Wnt brings Frizzled together with its single-pass co-receptor, LRP5 or LRP6.
cards.section: How Wnt slows destruction and flips TCF

cards.front: After Wnt brings Frizzled and LRP5/6 together, how is the β-catenin destruction complex inactivated?
cards.back: Frizzled recruits Dishevelled and the phosphorylated LRP6 tail binds Axin, pulling the destruction complex to the receptor so it stops delivering β-catenin to the ligase.
cards.why: How the complex is stopped is still argued, yet newly made β-catenin survives, builds up, and enters the nucleus.
cards.quote: Inside, Frizzled recruits Dishevelled, and the phosphorylated LRP6 tail binds Axin, pulling the destruction complex to the receptor so it stops delivering β-catenin to the ligase.
cards.section: How Wnt slows destruction and flips TCF

cards.front: How does nuclear β-catenin change the activity of DNA-bound TCF at Wnt target genes?
cards.back: When β-catenin arrives, the bound co-repressor (Groucho) leaves and β-catenin recruits transcription machinery, switching TCF from a repressor to an activator.
cards.why: The simple model is that β-catenin pushes Groucho off, though how Groucho is actually removed is still being worked out.
cards.quote: When β-catenin arrives, Groucho leaves and β-catenin recruits transcription machinery, turning TCF from repressor to activator.
cards.section: How Wnt slows destruction and flips TCF

cards.front: If different cell types share the same Wnt/β-catenin/TCF pathway, why do they switch on different sets of target genes?
cards.back: Which target genes answer depends in part on where TCF is already positioned on the DNA in that cell type.
cards.quote: Which genes answer depends in part on where TCF sits in that cell type.
cards.section: How Wnt slows destruction and flips TCF

cards.front: One common TCF target gene encodes Axin2, an Axin-like scaffold protein. If Wnt remains present for hours, what happens to free β-catenin levels, and why?
cards.back: Free β-catenin is pulled partway back down. Newly made Axin2 supplies extra scaffold that rebuilds destruction capacity, providing negative feedback that helps bound the response.
cards.quote: Pull it partway back down: extra Axin-like scaffold rebuilds destruction capacity
cards.section: How Wnt slows destruction and flips TCF

cards.front: Insulin activates Akt to switch GSK3 off. If cultured cells are treated with insulin alone (no Wnt), what happens to free β-catenin and TCF target genes, and why?
cards.back: In the cultured cells tested, insulin does not raise β-catenin or switch on TCF genes. The explanation offered is that Axin-bound GSK3 is a separate pool that Akt does not reach.
cards.quote: In the cultured cells tested, insulin does not raise β-catenin. The explanation offered is that Axin-bound GSK3 is a separate pool that Akt does not reach.
cards.section: How Wnt slows destruction and flips TCF

cards.front: Suppose a mutation removes the phosphorylation sites on the cytoplasmic tail of LRP6 so it can no longer bind Axin. What happens to free β-catenin when Wnt binds Frizzled and mutant LRP6, and why?
cards.back: In the lesson's model, free β-catenin stays low and Wnt signaling fails. Without the phosphorylated LRP6 tail binding Axin, the destruction complex is not pulled to the receptor and continues delivering β-catenin to the ubiquitin ligase.
cards.quote: the phosphorylated LRP6 tail binds Axin, pulling the destruction complex to the receptor so it stops delivering β-catenin to the ligase.
cards.section: How Wnt slows destruction and flips TCF

cards.front: Suppose a cell line cannot transcribe the Axin2 gene (an Axin-like scaffold) in response to TCF, while all other Wnt pathway parts are normal. Under hours of continuous Wnt exposure, how will free β-catenin differ from normal cells, and which two rules explain this?
cards.back: Free β-catenin will rise higher and stay elevated instead of dropping partway back down. By the Axin2 negative-feedback rule, normal cells rebuild destruction capacity over hours; by the first-order steady-state rule (steady level = synthesis ÷ destruction rate constant), losing that recovery keeps the destruction rate constant lower and the steady level higher.
cards.quote: One common TCF target gene is Axin2, a relative of Axin. If Wnt stays present for hours, what should new Axin2 do to the β-catenin level?
cards.section: How Wnt slows destruction and flips TCF

cards.front: Why do most people who inherit one faulty copy of APC develop hundreds to thousands of colon polyps (familial adenomatous polyposis)?
cards.back: Each colon cell is only one hit away from losing its remaining working copy of APC, which leaves β-catenin/TCF signaling stuck on without Wnt.
cards.why: Nearly all people with familial adenomatous polyposis develop colon cancer unless the colon is removed.
cards.quote: because each cell is one hit away from losing its remaining working copy; nearly all get colon cancer unless the colon is removed.
cards.section: Wnt in disease: a drain stuck shut

cards.front: Beyond inherited polyposis, APC is mutated in about {{c1::four in five}} sporadic colon cancers.
cards.quote: APC is also mutated in about four in five sporadic colon cancers.
cards.section: Wnt in disease: a drain stuck shut

cards.front: Colon cancer cells lacking functional APC show active β-catenin/TCF transcription with no Wnt added, and reintroducing functional APC shuts that transcription off. What does this result show?
cards.back: Functional APC is required to keep β-catenin/TCF transcription off without Wnt; loss of APC alone drives constitutive pathway activation in these cells.
cards.quote: colon cancer cells without working APC had β-catenin and TCF active all the time, and restoring APC shut that transcription off.
cards.section: Wnt in disease: a drain stuck shut

cards.front: How do some colon tumors with intact APC leave Wnt signaling stuck on, and how does the blocked step differ from APC loss?
cards.back: They mutate β-catenin's CK1/GSK3 phosphorylation sites so no β-TrCP tag forms. With APC loss, β-catenin is still phosphorylated, but ubiquitination handover and destruction become inefficient.
cards.quote: Some colon tumours with normal APC carried β-catenin mutations instead, at the CK1 and GSK3 phosphorylation sites.
cards.section: Wnt in disease: a drain stuck shut

cards.front: Newborn mice lacking TCF4 have no dividing compartment in the small intestine. What does this show about normal gut renewal, and how does APC loss mirror that biology?
cards.back: It shows that gut crypt-base stem cells and dividing cells above them depend on Wnt/TCF signaling. A colon cell that loses APC behaves as if it never left the crypt base.
cards.quote: Gut lining stem cells at the base of crypts and dividing cells above them depend on Wnt: newborn mice without TCF4 lack the dividing compartment of the small intestine.
cards.section: Wnt in disease: a drain stuck shut

cards.front: Two inactive copies of LRP5 cause fragile, low-density bone, whereas one change (glycine 171 to valine) produces unusually dense bone. Which direction does each push β-catenin signaling, and which matches losing APC?
cards.back: Inactive LRP5 lowers signaling (fragile bone), while glycine 171 to valine raises signaling (dense bone). The dense-bone variant matches the direction of APC loss, though it acts at the co-receptor rather than the destruction complex.
cards.quote: The same pathway sets bone mass: two inactive copies of LRP5 cause fragile, low-density bone, whereas one change (glycine 171 to valine) gives unusually dense bone.
cards.section: Wnt in disease: a drain stuck shut

cards.front: A drug blocks the enzyme that attaches the fatty acid to Wnt, stopping cells from secreting active Wnt. Predict its effect on β-catenin signaling in a colon tumor lacking both copies of APC, and state the pathway rule this rests on.
cards.back: It will have very little effect. By the canonical pathway order rule (Wnt → Frizzled/LRP5/6 → destruction complex → β-catenin), blocking Wnt secretion acts upstream of the receptor, whereas APC loss breaks the downstream destruction complex so β-catenin accumulates without Wnt.
cards.quote: Because Wnt raises free β-catenin by slowing its constant destruction, a mutation that slows destruction on its own can switch TCF on without Wnt.
cards.section: Wnt in disease: a drain stuck shut

cards.front: Two colon cancer cell lines show high TCF-driven reporter activity without Wnt. Introducing full-length APC sharply lowers reporter activity in Line A but leaves Line B unchanged. Using the destruction-complex rules, explain what defect fits each line.
cards.back: Line A lacks functional APC, so restoring APC repairs ubiquitination handover and clears β-catenin. Line B has functional APC but carries a β-catenin phosphorylation-site mutation; by the β-TrCP recognition rule, even a complete destruction complex cannot build the phosphate tag needed to mark that β-catenin for destruction.
cards.quote: colon cancer cells without working APC had β-catenin and TCF active all the time, and restoring APC shut that transcription off.
cards.section: Wnt in disease: a drain stuck shut

cards.front: A direction shared across the plane of a cell sheet—like fly wing hairs pointing toward the wing tip—is called {{c1::planar cell polarity}}.
cards.quote: A direction shared across the plane of a sheet—like fly wing hairs pointing toward the wing tip—is planar cell polarity (PCP).
cards.section: Planar cell polarity: how cells agree which way to point

cards.front: In normal fly wings, creating a small patch of frizzled-null cells causes genetically normal cells on the tip side of the patch to grow misdirected hairs, while normal cells on the body side stay normal. What do the misdirected normal cells show?
cards.back: Each cell learns its direction locally from the neighbors it touches rather than reading a whole-wing coordinate map on its own.
cards.why: Because genetically normal cells changed orientation solely due to adjacent mutant cells, directional information is passed across cell borders.
cards.quote: made patches of frizzled-null cells in normal wings: normal cells on the tip side grew misdirected hairs, while those on the other side did not.
cards.section: Planar cell polarity: how cells agree which way to point

cards.front: In fly wings, hairs point from cells with more Frizzled toward cells with less. If a patch of wing cells produces more Frizzled than normal, which side—body side or tip side—shows backward hairs on normal neighbors, and why?
cards.back: The body side. Normal neighbors point away from the high-Frizzled patch: tip-side neighbors still point tipward (normal), whereas body-side neighbors flip backward away from the patch.
cards.quote: Later work from Adler's lab showed that hairs point from cells with more Frizzled toward cells with less.
cards.section: Planar cell polarity: how cells agree which way to point

cards.front: In a fly wing cell undergoing planar cell polarity, where do Frizzled and Dishevelled, Van Gogh and Prickle, and Flamingo localize?
cards.back: Frizzled and Dishevelled sit on the tip-side edge (where the actin hair forms), Van Gogh and Prickle sit on the opposite edge, and Flamingo links every border.
cards.quote: In each wing cell, Frizzled and Dishevelled sit on the tip-side edge, Van Gogh and Prickle on the opposite edge, and the cadherin Flamingo links every border.
cards.section: Planar cell polarity: how cells agree which way to point

cards.front: Which core signaling components are shared between planar cell polarity and the β-catenin pathway, and which are excluded from planar cell polarity?
cards.back: Both use Frizzled and Dishevelled, whereas core planar cell polarity does not use LRP5/6, β-catenin, or TCF.
cards.quote: Each cell builds its actin hair on the Frizzled side—none of this uses β-catenin or TCF.
cards.section: Planar cell polarity: how cells agree which way to point

cards.front: Suppose a tissue loses both LRP5 and LRP6 while Frizzled and Dishevelled remain normal. Predict the effect on canonical β-catenin gene activation and on core planar cell polarity, and state the rules this rests on.
cards.back: Canonical β-catenin signaling is lost or sharply lowered, while core planar cell polarity is spared. By the canonical receptor rule, Wnt requires LRP5/6 so the phosphorylated co-receptor tail can bind Axin and halt β-catenin destruction; by the core PCP rule, Frizzled and Dishevelled align cells without LRP5/6, β-catenin, or TCF.
cards.quote: Each cell builds its actin hair on the Frizzled side—none of this uses β-catenin or TCF.
cards.section: Planar cell polarity: how cells agree which way to point

cards.front: What embryonic process uses planar cell polarity genes in vertebrates, and what defect results when PCP is disrupted?
cards.back: PCP guides narrowing, lengthening, and folding of the neural plate into the neural tube; disrupting it causes neural tube closure defects, including spina bifida.
cards.why: Mice with two mutant copies of Vangl2 keep the neural tube open along most of its length, and rare VANGL1 variants appear in some humans with neural tube defects.
cards.quote: Disrupting PCP causes neural tube closure defects, including spina bifida: mice with two mutant copies of Vangl2 (a vertebrate Van Gogh)
cards.section: Planar cell polarity: how cells agree which way to point

cards.front: Vertebrates require particular Wnts—including {{c1::Wnt5a and Wnt11}}—which is one reason planar cell polarity is counted as a Wnt pathway.
cards.quote: Vertebrates also require particular Wnts—Wnt5a and Wnt11 among them—one reason PCP is counted as a Wnt pathway.
cards.section: Planar cell polarity: how cells agree which way to point

cards.front: In the two-protein (A and B) planar polarity model, what two local membrane rules let cells align across a sheet given only a weak tissue bias?
cards.back: Between cells, A on one cell holds B on the touching neighbor across the gap; within each cell, A and B drive each other away so no edge keeps both.
cards.quote: Between cells, A on one cell holds B on the cell it touches, so each keeps the other in place across the gap.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In the two-protein (A/B) polarity model where hairs grow on the A side (A holds B across borders; A and B repel within a cell), a patch of cells lacks A. What happens to adjacent normal cells, and why is only one side reversed?
cards.back: Adjacent normal cells point their hairs toward the patch, flipping hairs backward on one side only. Cells without A display B on every edge, so normal neighbors gather A on the border touching the patch; on one side that matches the normal direction, and on the other side it points backward.
cards.quote: Each normal neighbour gathers its A on the edge that touches the patch, so its hair points toward the patch.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In the two-protein (A/B) planar polarity model (A = Frizzled side where the hair grows, B = Van Gogh side), predict how a patch of cells lacking B affects normal neighbors on each side, and state the rules this rests on.
cards.back: Normal neighbors point their hairs away from the B-null patch, reversing hairs on the opposite side from an A-null patch (the body side in a wing). By the within-cell exclusion rule, B-null cells display A on every edge; by the between-cell pairing rule, normal neighbors gather B facing the patch and push A—and their hairs—to the edge away from the patch.
cards.quote: Within a cell, A and B drive each other away, so no edge keeps both.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In mouse mammary tumors caused by a retrovirus that inserts a DNA provirus into chromosomes, 18 of 26 tumors had a provirus within one ~19 kb region, and tested tumors made RNA from that region while tested lactating mammary glands did not. What did this suggest?
cards.back: Repeated proviral insertions in one stretch of DNA, together with RNA made from that region in the tumours tested but not in the lactating glands tested, probably flag a cellular gene (int-1) that favors tumor growth when disturbed.
cards.quote: This retrovirus inserts a DNA copy (provirus) into mouse chromosomes; repeated insertions in one stretch of DNA probably flag a gene that favours tumour growth when disturbed.
cards.section: How int-1 and wingless became Wnt

cards.front: What connection between cancer and development emerged when the fly version of mouse int-1 proved to be wingless?
cards.back: One gene conserved across over 500 million years (54% identical, all 23 cysteines conserved) both patterns fly embryos and causes mouse mammary tumors when misexpressed.
cards.quote: One gene kept across more than 500 million years caused mouse tumours when misexpressed and patterned fly embryos.
cards.section: How int-1 and wingless became Wnt

cards.front: Strong loss-of-function mutations in fly wingless (Wnt) and armadillo (β-catenin) both cause the same embryonic segment-pattern defect. Based on canonical Wnt pathway rules, how would losing a destruction-complex member like Axin or APC affect pathway output compared with losing wingless?
cards.back: It would be expected to push pathway output in the opposite direction—stuck on instead of off. By the canonical Wnt rule, Wnt slows destruction to raise β-catenin, so losing wingless or armadillo shuts signaling off, whereas losing a destruction-complex member slows destruction on its own and would switch target genes on without Wnt (as shown for APC loss in colon cancer cells).
cards.quote: other fly mutants with the same segment defect—including armadillo, the fly's β-catenin—mapped the rest of the pathway.
cards.section: How int-1 and wingless became Wnt
